case_name: Kanakarajan @ Kanakan v State of Kerala
respondent:
State of Kerala
Supreme Court of India

21 April 2017
Criminal Appeal No. 841 of 2007
The Judgment was delivered by : N.V. Ramana, J.
1. This appeal is directed against the Judgment dated 8th November, 2006 passed by the High Court of Kerala in Criminal Appeal No. 1906 of 2004, wherein the High Court has dismissed the appeal preferred by the accused/appellant herein and upheld the order of conviction and sentence passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Fast Track Court-I, Palakkad, in Sessions Case No. 104 of 2002.

facts: The material available on record reveals that initially there were nine accused in this case against whom an FIR was registered at 9 am on 6.3.2000 at Kongad Police Station for causing the death of one Rajesh and injuring the complainant/Vinod (PW2), who happens to be the cousin of the deceased.

Since the accused No. 2 (Ayyappankutty) was found hanging from a tree on the next day and was declared dead, charges were framed only against the remaining accused under Sections 143, 147, 148, 302, 342 and 324 r/w 149 of Indian Penal Code, 1860 [hereafter 'IPC' for brevity].

The brief facts of the case as unfolded from the case of prosecution is that, on the intervening night of 5th and 6th March, 2000, an ox procession was going on at Kunnappully temple at Tharakassery and several people had gathered around the temple premises.
On the way to the Medical College, Rajesh succumbed to the injuries at about 5.30 A.M.
The prosecution in order to bring home the guilt of the accused has produced 23 witnesses and the defense has produced one witness.
Out of the aforesaid 23 prosecution witnesses, PW3 who was an eyewitness to the incident, turned hostile.
PWs 11 and 12, who were witnesses to the recovery mahazar (Ext. P10), also turned hostile.
At the alleged place of incident, which is a temple compound, there were more than 10,000 people present in addition to the police force stationed around the temple compound.
issues: Whether the High Court is justified in convicting the accused (A1)
Whether the prosecution could prove the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt?
petitioner_arguments: The entire case is fabricated and foisted one suppressing the real incident that had taken place in order to falsely implicate the accused/appellant.
When an incident of such grave nature had taken place amidst huge public gathering and police force, it is impossible to not have a single independent witness.
Making PW2 a witness to the alleged incident is an afterthought of prosecution.
There was an inordinate delay of 24 hours on the part of police in presenting the FIR before the court and no reason has been given by the prosecution for such delay.
The motive behind the crime, as alleged by the prosecution, is so trivial and unbelievable, would not be a sufficient reason for the accused to settle with such a heinous crime.
respondent_arguments: The reasoning given by the High Court in convicting the accused is based on settled legal principles.

The High Court clearly recorded the finding that though no reliance is placed on the testimony made by the prime witness (PW2), it may not make any difference in fastening the liability of the accused.
court_reasoning: Looking at the evidence on record we find that there are certain pivotal issues where the prosecution has failed to provide a satisfactory explanation.
The facts on hand reveal that the incident took place at 2 AM on the night of 5th and 6th March 2000.
Moreover PW2-the eye witness, who happens to be the cousin of the deceased, basing on whose information the criminal law was set into motion.
holding: The appeal of appellant/A1 was however dismissed by the High Court as being devoid of any merit, thereby confirming the order of conviction and sentence passed by the Trial Court.
